title: Multi-factor authentication adds another checkpoint
summary: Multi-factor authentication asks for more than a password. It can reduce the risk that a stolen password alone is enough to access an account.
body: A password is one kind of proof that you are the account holder. Multi-factor authentication adds another kind, such as a code, security key or device approval. This extra step can block some attacks that rely only on stolen passwords.

The methods are not all equally resistant to phishing. Where available, a passkey or hardware security key can provide stronger protection than a code entered into a website. An authenticator app can be a useful alternative. Text-message codes may be better than no additional factor, but can have weaknesses.

Treat unexpected sign-in approvals as warning signs. Do not approve a prompt you did not initiate or share a one-time code with someone who contacts you. Save recovery codes securely and review how to revoke devices you no longer use.
takeaways: Turn on MFA for email, financial and other important accounts.
Prefer phishing-resistant sign-in options where available.
Never approve an unexpected prompt or share a one-time code.
